what_it_does: Modern chips pack different types of processing cores on the same die — some optimized for performance, others for efficiency — plus voltage-and-frequency knobs that trade speed for power. Figuring out which core and which power setting to use for each moment of an application is hard, especially when multiple programs run at once and compete for shared resources like caches and memory bandwidth (resource contention). EffiCast frames this as a prediction problem: given past measurements of how efficiently the system has been running, forecast what the near future will look like, then pre-tune resources accordingly. It uses two types of sequence-modeling neural networks — LSTM (long short-term memory, a network good at learning patterns in time-series data) and Transformer (the architecture behind modern AI chat models) — trained on traces that capture efficiency across different core types, power settings, application phases, and contention patterns. The model produces a forecast in about 1.8 milliseconds, fast enough to act on it in real time.
